clue.text: As regards drugs, they have their scruples

definitions.text: As regards drugs, they have their scruples

parts.words: As regards drugs, they have their scruples
parts.note: a scruple is a unit in the old ...' weight system, so the old dispensing chemists literally kept scruples among their measures

explanation.surface: People in the drugs business turn out to have a conscience after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scruples' looks like moral qualms, but a scruple is also a twenty-grain weight used by old dispensing chemists.
explanation.definitionFit: The old dispensing chemists who measured out drugs used a weight system containing scruples.

clue.text: what an apprentice steeplejack to

parts.note: the printed clue has two blanks filled by one word: first split as an article plus church towers (what the trainee climbs), then read whole as a verb meaning aims high

explanation.surface: Fill in the blanks about the ambitions of a trainee steeple-climber.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue reads '— what an apprentice steeplejack — to': the same seven letters fill both blanks, the first time split as A SPIRES (what he climbs), the second as one verb meaning aims high.
explanation.definitionFit: A steeplejack climbs church towers, and to be ambitious is to set one's sights high on those very towers.

clue.text: Look up to an old French soldier in Cowper's place

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' tells us to read the word for look from bottom to top

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold
Michel Ney was one of Napoleon's marshals

explanation.surface: Someone gazes up at a veteran of Napoleon's army in the poet's home town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns LO into OL. The poet William Cowper lived for many years in this Buckinghamshire market town.
explanation.definitionFit: The eighteenth-century poet William Cowper lived in this English town and wrote hymns there.

clue.text: Manège verging on the unmanageable ?

definitions.meaning: manège is the art of training and riding horses, so it is play with horses
rough-and-tumble fun that is close to getting out of hand

explanation.surface: Riding-school exercises that are close to running out of control.
explanation.walkthrough: Manège is the French-derived word for a riding school and its exercises, read here as 'play' involving horses.
explanation.definitionFit: Equestrian exercise is literally play with mounts, while boisterous roughhousing is close to getting out of hand.

clue.text: What to do if you're fed up to the teeth

definitions.text: What to do if you're fed up to the teeth

parts.words: What to do if you're fed up to the teeth
parts.note: 'fed up to the teeth' sounds like utter exasperation, but read literally it means food has been brought up to the mouth, where it is ground

explanation.surface: Advice for someone who has had absolutely enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fed up to the teeth' is an idiom for exasperation; taken literally it describes food delivered to the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that reaches the teeth is next ground by the jaws before swallowing.

clue.text: The Ark's wireless operator?

parts.note: Noah's son Ham sailed on the Ark, and an amateur wireless operator is called by that same name

explanation.surface: A whimsical question about who handled communications aboard Noah's vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: Ham was one of Noah's three sons aboard the Ark; an amateur radio enthusiast is also called a ham.
explanation.definitionFit: An amateur wireless enthusiast is the everyday phrase, and Ham was a passenger of the Ark.

clue.text: One banished from Corsica, say

indicators.note: 'say' signals that the phrase is to be spoken, giving a word that sounds like it

parts.note: 'from' is ex and Corsica is an island, or isle, so 'from Corsica' is ex-isle

explanation.surface: Someone driven out of Napoleon's home island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from Corsica' becomes ex-isle (out of the island), and 'say' turns that into the sound of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A person sent away from their homeland by decree lives in banishment.

clue.text: Mum's to put on something found in a Mammoth Sale ?

definitions.text: something found in a Mammoth Sale ?

parts.note: ma is mum, so mum's is ma's
to don a garment is to put it on

explanation.surface: Mother is getting dressed for a huge bargain sale.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'Mammoth Sale' sounds like a giant clearance, but here it is a sale of mammoths and their extinct relatives.
explanation.definitionFit: This extinct elephant-like beast is a close cousin of the woolly mammoth.

clue.text: Weedy-looking horse

definitions.meaning: a common weedy plant of meadows and dock-like leaves
a horse of a reddish-brown colour is named for that colour

explanation.surface: A feeble, scrawny-looking nag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weedy' looks like puny, but it points to the plant: the same word names a leafy herb and a chestnut-coloured horse.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a sour-leaved meadow herb and a reddish-brown horse.

clue.text: Lady Swan is amiable but somewhat distant

definitions.text: Lady Swan is amiable but somewhat distant

parts.words: Lady Swan is amiable but somewhat distant
parts.note: a pen is a female swan, and a friend who is warm but far away writes letters

explanation.surface: A society lady named Swan is pleasant yet aloof.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Swan looks like a name, but a female swan is a pen; add an amiable companion who stays at a distance, known only by letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A correspondent one befriends by post is friendly yet usually lives far away.

clue.text: State in which I had a home taken from me

parts.note: I had contracts to I'd

indicators.note: something taken from another word is removed from it, here the word for me

parts.note: taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: Someone recalls an American state where their house was confiscated.
explanation.walkthrough: I'D + A + HOME, then 'taken from' removes ME, leaving HO at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A US state in the Pacific Northwest, famous for potatoes.

clue.text: Thomas whose verse was not blank

definitions.text: Thomas whose verse was not blank

parts.words: Thomas whose verse was not blank
parts.note: Thomas of Erceldoune, the Scottish seer, is known by an epithet saying his verse chimed; blank verse is verse without chimes

explanation.surface: A poet named Thomas who did not write in unrhymed lines.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas of Erceldoune, a thirteenth-century Scottish poet and prophet, is known in ballad as Thomas the ___; blank verse is unrhymed.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse that is not blank has chiming line endings, the craft of a versifier named for it.

clue.text: Author concerned with 23's book

definitions.meaning: C. S. ... wrote the Hornblower novels
John Evelyn (23 across) wrote Sylva, a book on tree-growing, so someone concerned with it tends woodland

explanation.surface: A writer who took an interest in another man's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 23 across is EVELYN: John Evelyn's Sylva (1664) was a treatise on growing trees.
explanation.definitionFit: C. S. Forester was a novelist, and a woodland keeper looks after the trees Evelyn wrote about.

clue.text: Leathery bit of old sheep ?

parts.note: a riding seat is made of leather, and a joint of mutton (meat from an older sheep) cut across the back has the same name

explanation.surface: A tough cut of meat from an aged animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The word names both the leather seat on a horse and a butcher's cut of mutton from the back.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider's seat is leather, and a back joint of mutton bears the same name.

clue.text: These financial savings are having precipitate

definitions.meaning: money placed in a bank account
sediment that settles out of a liquid

explanation.surface: Bank savings are suddenly being rushed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'precipitate' looks like hasty, but here it is the chemist's noun: solid matter that settles out.
explanation.definitionFit: Money placed in a bank and sediment settling out of a liquid share the same name.

clue.text: March-time trumpeter

parts.note: a trumpeter at march time sounds like a military bandsman, but this is a spring flower with a trumpet-shaped centre that blooms in March

explanation.surface: A bugler in a marching band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March-time' suggests marching tempo; it is the month, when this trumpet-shaped yellow flower blooms.
explanation.definitionFit: This yellow spring bulb has a trumpet-shaped corona and flowers in March.

clue.text: Of which the Ballad of Reading Gaol is no example

definitions.text: Of which the Ballad of Reading Gaol is no example

parts.words: Of which the Ballad of Reading Gaol is no example
parts.note: Oscar Wilde's prison poem is in strict rhyme and metre, and being about a gaol it is also hardly about liberty

explanation.surface: A remark about the form of Oscar Wilde's prison poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilde's Ballad of Reading Gaol is rhymed and metrical, so it is not unrhymed poetry, and as a prison poem it is not 'free' either.
explanation.definitionFit: Poetry without regular rhyme or metre is the opposite of Wilde's tightly rhymed ballad.

clue.text: Mr Darling's disgrace

parts.note: in Peter Pan, Mr Darling lives in Nana's kennel as penance after his children fly away

explanation.surface: The shame of a family man in a children's story.
explanation.walkthrough: In J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan, Mr Darling punishes himself by living in the dog's kennel; to be 'in the dog-house' is to be in disgrace.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the kennel is an idiom for being out of favour, and Mr Darling literally lived in one.

clue.text: Something of his waggishness in your make-up, little boy

definitions.text: Something of his waggishness in your make-up, little boy

parts.words: Something of his waggishness in your make-up, little boy
parts.note: waggishness sounds like playful humour, but it is the tail-wagging of a young hound, whose eager charm a small boy shares

explanation.surface: A fond remark that a small lad has a playful streak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waggishness' suggests joking; here it is tail-wagging, as in the eager, soulful look of a young dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A young hound wags eagerly, and a little boy can show the same playful devotion.

clue.text: Adorable apple-woman

parts.note: 'adorable' here means fit to be worshipped: the Roman goddess of fruit trees and orchards

explanation.surface: A charming woman selling apples.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adorable' means worthy of adoration: the Roman goddess of fruit and orchards, often shown with apples.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman deity of orchards was worshipped, and her emblem was fruit such as apples.

clue.text: Brown's grot that's green

parts.note: T. E. Brown's poem My Garden lists 'Rose plot, Fringed pool, Fern'd grot', a grotto made green by its leafy plants

explanation.surface: A shady green grotto belonging to someone called Brown.
explanation.walkthrough: T. E. Brown, a Manx poet, wrote 'A garden is a lovesome thing, God wot! Rose plot, Fringed pool, Fern'd grot'.
explanation.definitionFit: A grotto overgrown with fronds is green, as in the poet's line.

clue.text: Of a sudden 'e madly strips

indicators.note: letters behaving madly are thrown into disorder and rearranged

parts.note: 'e is he with the h dropped, a lone letter e

explanation.surface: A Cockney man suddenly tears off his clothes in a frenzy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'madly' rearranges SUDDEN plus E. ''e' is the dropped-h spelling of he, so it supplies only the letter E.
explanation.definitionFit: To strip something bare is to lay it naked, removing its covering.

clue.text: With this spell, however stiff the upper lip, it has to be painful

definitions.text: With this spell, however stiff the upper lip

parts.note: must means has to
to ache is to be painful

explanation.surface: Even a stoic with a stiff upper lip must admit it hurts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With this spell' points to the shorter American spelling, without the O, of the hair on the upper lip.
explanation.definitionFit: Facial hair grown on the upper lip, here in the American spelling.

clue.text: 13 beheaded — that's bad

indicators.note: a word beheaded loses its first letter

parts.note: 13 across is the leather seat for riding, also a cut of mutton

explanation.surface: Something numbered thirteen has its head cut off, which is unfortunate.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 across is SADDLE; 'beheaded' removes its first letter, the S.
explanation.definitionFit: An addled egg is rotten, so the word can mean spoiled or gone off.

clue.text: Hope expired for man of the trees

definitions.meaning: Browning's poem begins 'Beautiful ... Hope is dead!'
John ..., the diarist, wrote Sylva, a treatise on forest trees

explanation.surface: Hope ran out for a tree-lover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hope' looks like the feeling, but it is the surname of the dead girl in Browning's poem 'Evelyn Hope'.
explanation.definitionFit: Browning's dead girl had this first name, and the seventeenth-century diarist who wrote Sylva had it as surname.

clue.text: What is a man at when he's wanted ?

definitions.text: What is a man at when he's wanted ?

parts.words: What is a man at when he's wanted ?
parts.note: 'wanted' reads as desired, but here it means sought by the police: such a fugitive is still free and roaming

explanation.surface: A question about where someone is when people are looking for him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanted' means sought by the police; an escaped criminal who has not been caught is said to be 'at ___'.
explanation.definitionFit: A fugitive on the run is free, the idiom being at liberty or uncaptured.

clue.text: Arrange, report of what happened at high watermark

definitions.text: Arrange, report of what happened at high watermark

parts.words: Arrange, report of what happened at high watermark
parts.note: to arrange a report for publication is the ... task, and at high water the tide turns: that word read backwards gives the letters

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to prepare an account of events at the flood line.
explanation.walkthrough: At high water the tide turns, so 'what happened' is TIDE read backwards; 'Arrange, report' points to preparing copy for print.
explanation.definitionFit: Preparing written copy for publication means revising and arranging it.

clue.text: Observed, looking back, to begin to explode

indicators.note: looking back tells us to read the shortened word from right to left
only the beginning of the word for explode is used, its ending dropped

parts.note: to detonate is to explode

explanation.surface: Someone, glancing over their shoulder, saw a bomb about to go off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to begin' keeps DETON from DETONATE, dropping ATE; 'looking back' turns DETON round.
explanation.definitionFit: Something seen and remarked on has been taken note of.

clue.text: Like mermaids and mongrels ?

parts.note: mermaids are born and raised beneath the waves, while mongrels are of low pedigree: one word covers both

explanation.surface: A comparison of sea-maidens and mixed-breed dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two parts the word says raised below (the sea); read as one it means of poor breeding, like a mongrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Mongrels lack good pedigree, and mermaids are reared beneath the sea.

clue.text: Yet contradicts law of diminishing returns

definitions.meaning: yet in the sense of however or all the same
the law says returns grow smaller; split into three words, the answer denies that they ever get smaller

explanation.surface: But this defies the economists' law that extra effort yields less.
explanation.walkthrough: The law of diminishing returns says gains shrink; split into three words, the answer states the gains never shrink.
explanation.definitionFit: Yet and however both introduce a contrast, as does this conjunction meaning all the same.
